items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Almighty God, humbly acknowle dging our need for Thy guidance
in all things, and laying aside all private and personal interests, we beseech Thee to
grant that we may conduct the affairs of this  House and of our country to the glory of
Thy holy name, the maintenance of true re ligion and justice, the honour of the Queen,
and the public welfare and well-being of those still missing and suffering such trauma in
Canterbury today, through Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.
VISITORS
Commonwealth Parliamentary Association—United Kingdom Branch

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I have much pleasure in informing the House that a parliamentary
delegation from the Commonwealth Parliame ntary Association branch of the United
Kingdom, led by the Rt Hon Sir Alan Beith, is present in the gallery. I am sure members
would wish that the delegation be welcomed.
Earthquake—Christchurch
Hon BILL ENGLISH (Deputy Prime Minister)  on behalf of the Prime Minister:
I wish to make a ministerial statement. T oday we would as a Parliament particularly
want to mark the tragic loss of life and injury that has occurred as a result of the
earthquake in Canterbury yesterday, to express our deepest sympathy to the families,
friends, and colleagues of those who have di ed and those who are still missing, and to
acknowledge the work of the rescue teams wh o are working so hard in very difficult
circumstances.
Yesterday was indeed one of New Zealand’s da rkest days. It is hard to believe that
this Parliament is again assembling to ma rk another tragedy, a lthough the scale and
severity of this second Christchurch eart hquake is so far beyond our experience that
only the pictures can capture the horrendous  scale and impact of the disaster. Our
thoughts and our hearts turn to the people of  Christchurch who know they have lost
loved ones. To grieving mothers and fathers,  brothers and sisters,  sons and daughters,
partners and friends, I say please accept our condolences, our sympathy, and our support
on behalf of all New Zealanders. To those who wait anxiously to hear news of those
who are missing, I say we feel their anxiet y, and we know that as the hours pass their
anxiety will grow and so will ours. We are a small, close-knit country, and many people
stand with them while they wait. Let me  repeat the assurance given by the Prime

items.speaker: Minister earlier today
items.text: no one will be left to walk this journey alone; New Zealand will
walk this journey with them.
The focus right now is on saving lives, resc uing those who are trapped, and treating
those who are injured. Already we have witnes sed some inspirational stories of rescue.
Of course, there are many stories yet untol d of workers and passers-by helping their
mates and strangers alike, and saving lives.  Those efforts, and the efforts of many
hundreds of courageous search and rescue workers, emergency personnel, medical
professionals, and others will continue for as long as it takes.
Government agencies, working with other groups, have moved swiftly to get people
and resources into Christchur ch to lead and su pport the rescue effo rt. That includes
about 100 New Zealand search and rescue specialists on the ground in Christchurch.
They are being joined today by two Australi an search and rescue teams of about 150
people in total. We have 600 military st aff on the ground, and the Defence Force has
16944 Ministerial Statements 23 Feb 2011
several ships and aircraft in the area. In addition to the Christchurch police force, over
230 extra police staff are arriving from other districts. Some arrived last night, and
others are arriving throughout today. Medical st aff have come into Christchurch from
around New Zealand and Australia. Many thousands of volunteers are lending a hand in
the best way that they know how. This Parl iament should have the reassurance that
every possible resource, not just nationally but  globally, that is relevant to securing the
lives of people affected by this earthquake is in Christchurch, or is on the way there.
I acknowledge the generous offers of sy mpathy and support we have received from
around the world. The Queen has conveyed he r deepest sympathy to the families and
friends of those who have been killed. Au stralian Prime Minister Julia Gillard has
expressed her condolences and has made a num ber of concrete offers of assistance,
which we have accepted. President Obama,  British Prime Mini ster Cameron, and
Canadian Prime Minister Harper have joined  other world leaders in expressing their
personal sympathy at our nation’s loss. We have  also received generous offers of help
from many of our internationa l friends. We have accepted offers from Australia, the
United States, Singapore, Japan, the United Ki ngdom, and Taiwan. We are continuing
to assess the requirements of Christchurch an d other offers of help that have come in,
which we will keep under review.
We know many people around the world are anxious to cont act family and friends
who are visiting or living in Christchurch. We are in close contact with foreign missions
in New Zealand, and I want to assure thos e countries—those who have offered help and
those who have nationals in New Zealand—that we are making every attempt we can to
find and identify their people.
It is a time for all of us to focus on saving lives and helping the people of
Christchurch. Other questions have arisen as  a result of the earthquake. We have been
asked about the likely economic impact of what has happened. It is really too soon to
look at these questions in de tail, but we want to reassu re New Zealanders that the
Earthquake Commission, the Gove rnment, Crown agencies, and private insurers have
all assured us that they have  the resources to meet thes e challenges and the will to
overcome them. I am absolutely confident that our community and our economy have
the resilience to come through th is. It will be a priority fo r this Government to recover
from the Christchurch earthquake.
Our immediate and pressing priority right now, though, is the people of Christchurch,
who desperately need our help. In the previous 6 months th ey have endured more pain,
more anxiety, and more heartache than most of us would have to endure over a lifetime,
and they are being called on again for more endurance. As a fello w South Islander, I
know that the people of Christchurch will have the spirit to come through this. The
traditional South Island grittiness will stand them in good stead. But, of course, they
need our support, and we want to absolutely reassure them that th ey have our support.
We will see lives today that are shattered, br ittle, and anxious, but  those lives will be
rebuilt tomorrow. In the last 2 days we have seen a city destroyed, but it will be rebuilt
for tomorrow. The Government and all of New Zealand will do ev erything possible to
make that happen.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: Yesterday we stood in this
House hoping against hope that the developi ng situation in Christchurch, following a
violent 6.3 earthquake at  12.50 p.m., would see l ittle loss of life, that we would once
again come through, and that the people of Christchurch, who had been through so
much, would be spared again. That was not to be. We are told that 75 people are now
confirmed dead. At each hour the gravity of this quake is increasing and dawning on
people all around the country. Many lives have been lost. Many people have been
injured, displaced, and severely traumatised. I think it is a disaster and a tragedy on a
23 Feb 2011 Ministerial Statements 16945
scale that most of us have never experi enced. For so many the nightmare goes on, with
aftershocks continuing as we speak.
There are few words to express the shock and distress that so many of us feel for the
people of Canterbury. Mr Speaker, I thank you for including your thoughts in the prayer
today. I have not heard that from the Chair in my time in Parliament. It shows the
feeling of this House towards the people of Canterbury.
To look at the frightened and bewildered  faces of fellow New Zealanders—our own
people—and particularly at the faces of ch ildren as they try to comprehend what has
happened leaves us all feeling helpless and powerless against such violent forces of
nature. Our sympathies, thoughts, and best wishes go out to the people of Canterbury, to
their families—in many cases in this House,  to our families—to their friends, and to
their neighbours. If only we could make it go away. The lifeline for many people who
are now waiting anxiously to hear about their families and friends is the courage and the
commitment of those undertaking the rescue  of people who are st ill trapped beneath
buildings that have collapse d. Their situation is danger ous, with debris falling and
buildings barely holding together, while quake s continue all the while. They are risking
their safety for fellow Kiwis. Each rescue is  a triumph and we greet  it with relief and
joy.
We have been joined, as the Deputy Prime Minister has said, by international rescue
teams and medical teams from around the worl d, particularly the Pa cific Basin, and we
thank them for their help. Only last week, in  this debating chamber, Julia Gillard said
that in a time of disaster we reach out to each other. Little did we know that we would
need their help so soon. So I thank our Aust ralian family for coming so quickly to our
aid. The emerging tales of surv ival and heroism after so ma ny hours is really heartfelt,
and we hope there will be many more in the hours ahead.
To all those on the ground working to rescue, to shelter, to fee d, and to comfort and
care for people in Christchurch, this House says thank you; our thoughts and prayers are
with you. As in any disaster, it is the days  afterwards that will bring home the cold
reality of the situation—when the impact on children will start to show, when the
pressure will mount for action and answer s, when support and generosity will be
needed. Let us continue to offer all we can in the days and months and years ahead. We
will need to open our wallets, our homes, our time, and our hearts. This is not a local
disaster and tragedy; it is our disaster, and it is our tragedy.
I thank the Ministers who this morning gave a briefing to members of this House and
to staff members. Open and honest communicati on will be the greatest help that can be
given to people in the days ahead. Once agai n, I thank the Christchurch members of
Parliament across this House who are on the ground right now working with their
people, as we would expect them to do and as they have done over the last 6 months.
The Labour Opposition passes on our deep  sympathy and condolences and thoughts
to the people of Canterbury at this time.

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: Let me first acknowledge the deaths that
we have seen in Christchurch. The Green Party of Aotearoa / New Zealand sends its
deepest sympathy and love to all of the fa milies and friends of those loved ones who
have been lost. No doubt there will be more  such families and friends and grief, and no
New Zealander will be spared an associati on with someone they know or care for who
has been so badly affected.
I want to acknowledge the Prime Minister and the Government Ministers for their
efforts in keeping members of Parliament br iefed on what is happening in Canterbury
and the ways that members of Parliament  and our staff can support those who need
support in Canterbury. This is  important not only so that MPs know how we can assist
16946 Ministerial Statements 23 Feb 2011
but so that those on the ground know that they have access to all of us and that we will
all be able to assist in one way or another.
It is important to acknowledge and thank all of those who are engaged in such
minute-by-minute heroic acts in Canterbury and Christchurch at the moment, who are
making such amazing efforts to rescue peopl e, and who are carin g for people who so
badly need it—the firefighters,  the police, the rescue teams,  all of the various forms of
health workers, the volunteers, the commun ity organisations, marae, and everyone who
is in Christchurch at the moment providing support to those who need it the most.
On behalf of the Green Party I want to ple dge ourselves to help in whatever way we
can, from all the different ways that it is possible to help. Our Christchurch-based MP,
Kennedy Graham, is in Christchurch now and is also available to assist those in
Canterbury and those who are working so hard to rescue people.
Finally, I acknowledge again th at our thoughts and our hearts  are with all those who
are in grief, with all those who are in pa in today, and with all those in New Zealand
who, as we have seen, are offering their best wishes to those in Canterbury. We want to
tell the people of Canterbury that they are not alone. Kia ora.

items.speaker: Hon RODNEY HIDE
items.text: Tragically, this is the darkest and grimmest
time of our lives for our country. The images on our television sets, the radio reports,
and the newspaper reports will be burnt into our minds forever, and will never be
forgotten. We look back to 4 September, and th e thing that strikes us  is that the images
were all about buildings; the images this tim e are all about people. We are reminded in
New Zealand of how close-knit we are, becaus e there is not a New Zealander, here or
overseas, who is not affected by a loved one, by a family member, by a friend, or by a
colleague missing or tragically killed.
It is important that the people of Chri stchurch know that they are not alone. We
know that their neighbours are looking out for them, complete strangers in the street are
looking out for them and doing their utmost, and the authorities and the emergency
crews are doing everything in their power. But the people of  Christchurch are also not
alone because all of New Zealand has stopped in its tracks, and our thoughts and our
prayers are with them.
Here in the House of Representatives, in  the people’s place, the Speaker, in an
unprecedented way, has put the people of Christ church into the prayer of Parliament.
There is now no political divi de in our Parliament as al l political parties support the
Government in this hour of need, and support the people of Christchurch.
It is not the case that just all of New Zealand is behind the people of Christchurch;
now all of the world is behi nd the people of New Zealand in  this truly tragic hour. We
are seeing New Zealanders now at their best as we dig deep for the sake of our loved
ones, for the sake of our community, and for the sake of our country, remembering
always that it is people who matter and how trifling are so many of the things that
concern us day to day; now those things just do not matter. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon Dr PITA SHARPLES
items.text: T ēnā koe, Mr Speaker.
Tēnā tātou. Ka hinga te tanga ta, ka heke iho ng ā hūpē, ngā roimata. Ka ringihia ki raro
ki te papa. When someone dies, our mucus and our tears flow down to the ground. It is a
display of our grief, and our connection to  those who pass away. There is hardly a
person who has not felt the need to cry over the tragedy that has happened in Ōtautahi—
Christchurch. In the last 24 hours what has been shown to us on the screens, on the
radio, and so on has revealed the true horror of the scope and scale of the tragedy that
has befallen our big city, Ōtautahi.
We all have connections to Ōtautahi—Christchurch. Whether it is whakapapa,
genealogy, friendship through sport, leisure, or work, we all have connections, and
those connections bind us at this time. Those connections make this whole situation
23 Feb 2011 Ministerial Statements 16947
very tender for us to carry, but they also un ite us and make us very strong, and confirm
our obligation to be involved—to be involved  by assisting in any way we can, by being
involved in our prayers and in our feelings for our people there, and our tears are for
those who have passed away.
I have been overwhelmed, honestly, by th e way the people of New Zealand have
rallied around to help in whichever way they can. The offers of help from overseas,
from so many countries that I did not beli eve even knew we existed, but which have
offered all sorts of help for us at this time, are really great. I would also like to
acknowledge my own M āori people for coming to the fore. Tomorrow we will meet in

items.speaker: Ōtautahi
items.text: Māori tribal leaders, M āori wardens, M āori incorporations, and the marae of
the South Island. Rehua Marae has made itsel f available as a hub from which activities
can flow. There have been promises of food to come into the area. The maraes of the
South Island, from Invercargill right up through Nelson and into Wellington, have made
themselves available for people who wish to be away from Christchurch at this time and
for those who are in need of accommodation. We  will support that with some financial
support to help those marae cope.
It is like everybody is doing something. Everybody feels the need to be involved, and
that is the same spirit with which the meeting will happen tomorrow in Ōtautahi, then a
further meeting in Auckland the next da y to look at other ways in which M āori can
show New Zealand we care—not just about M āori; we care about New Zealand. It is an
opportunity for everyone to be involved in that activity.
Ki ngā mate, haere, okioki pai mai me ng ā hūpē, me ng ā roimata o m ātou. Ki ng ā
whānau pani, koutou kua pania e ng ā mate nei, anei r ā mātou ki te tautoko i a koutou
kia whakamāmā i te wāhanga kei runga i ō koutou pokohiwi. It is with our tears and our
mucus that we show our regard for those who have passed away. May they rest in
peace. We also acknowledge the families who bear  the brunt of the sorrow at this time.
They should know that New Zealand cries a nd mourns with them. We share this, and
may this lift part of the load of grief th at they carry on their shoulders. Thank you. Kia
ora.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I acknowledge other party leaders
for their comments and for thei r contribution to Pa rliament’s expression of support for
the people of Christchurch. The Government will endeavour to keep MPs as closely
informed as is possible, not only about the re scue effort but also about the developing
processes for restarting the recovery effort in Christchurch. As it happens, because of all
the work that went in after the first earthquake , there is probably a clearer path forward,
even if the task of recovery is now much greater than it was earlier.
I re-emphasise the support of Parliament for those families who have lost loved ones
or will discover in the next week or so that they have lost loved ones. I pay tribute on
behalf of Parliament to those people who have led the rescue effort in Christchurch, at a
time when they often have not known what has happened with their own families. Many
people in Government agencies who have been  leading the rescue effort have put the
collective will ahead of finding out what has happened in their own situation, and they
deserve special acknowledgment.
Part of the task of Parliament and of politicians, in our role as community leaders,
while Christchurch is dealing with the shatteri ng effect of this devastating event, will
be—for those of us who are less directly affected by it—to move pretty quickly to think
about the future, and about the rebuilding effort  that the Prime Minist er talked about in
his comments today.
16948 Ministerial Statements 23 Feb 2011
Earthquake, Christchurch—State of National Emergency

items.speaker: Hon JOHN CARTER
items.text: I wish to make a ministerial
statement under Standing Order 347 in relation to the declaration of a state of national
emergency. On the advice of the Director of Civil Defence Emergency Management,
and in consultation with the Prime Minister  and the Mayor of Ch ristchurch, at 10.30
a.m. I declared a state of national emergenc y for Christchurch City, under section 66 of
the Civil Defence Emergency Management Act 2002. That step was taken as a result of
the magnitude 6.3 earthquake that occurred in Christchurch yesterday at 12.51 p.m., and
the continuing aftershocks.
This is the first time in New Zealand’s hi story that a state of national emergency has
been declared as a result of a civil defence emergency event. I took this step because I
considered the emergency to be of such a degree that the required civil defence
emergency management would be beyond the capacity of local civil defence emergency
people to respond to on thei r own. Under the Civil Defence Emergency Management
Act this declaration means that the Direct or of Civil Defence Emergency Management
may control the exercise and performance of  the functions, duties, and powers of the
civil defence emergency management groups and group controllers. There is no other
difference between the powers under a state of  local emergency and a state of national
emergency. The declaration of a state of national emergency will ensure the maximum
possible coordination and c ooperation between central and local resources and
international assistance. It also demonstrat es the Government’s commitment to help
people in Canterbury to respond to this disaster.
Like the Deputy Prime Minister, I wish to pay tribute to those personnel who work in
civil defence in Canterbury, and in all the ag encies that are working with them. As has
already been said, often they are working to  help other people wh ile they are dealing
with personal issues in relation to their own circumstances. I also pay tribute to the
Australian search and rescue parties w ho are already on the ground in Christchurch.
Teams from the United States, Singapore, the United Kingdom, Japan, and Taiwan will
be deployed as soon as  they get here. Offers of earthqu ake and rescue sp ecialists have
also been received from Belgium, Israel , the European Union, Greece, Malaysia,
Argentina, and France. The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian
Affairs has offered assistance, and Internat ional Search and Rescue Advisory Group
teams have been mobilised. An offer of assistance has been received from the United
Nations Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific.
As we consider this statement our t houghts are with the pe ople in Canterbury,
particularly with those who have lost loved ones and with loved ones still missing.

who are visiting or living in Christchurch. We are in close contact with foreign missions 
in New Zealand, and I want to assure thos e countries—those who have offered help and 
those who have nationals in New Zealand—that we are making every attempt we can to 
find and identify their people.  
It is a time for all of us to focus on saving lives and helping the people of 
Christchurch. Other questions have arisen as  a result of the earthquake. We have been 
asked about the likely economic impact of what has happened. It is really too soon to 
look at these questions in de tail, but we want to reassu re New Zealanders that the 
Earthquake Commission, the Gove rnment, Crown agencies, and private insurers have 
all assured us that they have  the resources to meet thes e challenges and the will to 
overcome them. I am absolutely confident that our community and our economy have 
the resilience to come through th is. It will be a priority fo r this Government to recover 
from the Christchurch earthquake.  
Our immediate and pressing priority right now, though, is the people of Christchurch, 
who desperately need our help. In the previous 6 months th ey have endured more pain, 
more anxiety, and more heartache than most of us would have to endure over a lifetime, 
and they are being called on again for more endurance. As a fello w South Islander, I 
know that the people of Christchurch will have the spirit to come through this. The 
traditional South Island grittiness will stand them in good stead. But, of course, they 
need our support, and we want to absolutely reassure them that th ey have our support. 
We will see lives today that are shattered, br ittle, and anxious, but  those lives will be 
rebuilt tomorrow. In the last 2 days we have seen a city destroyed, but it will be rebuilt 
for tomorrow. The Government and all of New Zealand will do ev erything possible to 
make that happen. 
Hon ANNETTE KING (Deputy Leader—Labour) : Yesterday we stood in this

injured, displaced, and severely traumatised. I think it is a disaster and a tragedy on a

teams and medical teams from around the worl d, particularly the Pa cific Basin, and we

MINISTERIAL STATEMENTS 
Earthquake, Christchurch—State of National Emergency 
Hon JOHN CARTER (Minister of Civil Defence) : I wish to make a ministerial 
statement under Standing Order 347 in relation to the declaration of a state of national 
emergency. On the advice of the Director of Civil Defence Emergency Management, 
and in consultation with the Prime Minister  and the Mayor of Ch ristchurch, at 10.30 
a.m. I declared a state of national emergenc y for Christchurch City, under section 66 of 
the Civil Defence Emergency Management Act 2002. That step was taken as a result of 
the magnitude 6.3 earthquake that occurred in Christchurch yesterday at 12.51 p.m., and 
the continuing aftershocks.  
This is the first time in New Zealand’s hi story that a state of national emergency has 
been declared as a result of a civil defence emergency event. I took this step because I 
considered the emergency to be of such a degree that the required civil defence 
emergency management would be beyond the capacity of local civil defence emergency 
people to respond to on thei r own. Under the Civil Defence Emergency Management 
Act this declaration means that the Direct or of Civil Defence Emergency Management 
may control the exercise and performance of  the functions, duties, and powers of the 
civil defence emergency management groups and group controllers. There is no other 
difference between the powers under a state of  local emergency and a state of national 
emergency. The declaration of a state of national emergency will ensure the maximum 
possible coordination and c ooperation between central and local resources and 
international assistance. It also demonstrat es the Government’s commitment to help 
people in Canterbury to respond to this disaster.  
Like the Deputy Prime Minister, I wish to pay tribute to those personnel who work in 
civil defence in Canterbury, and in all the ag encies that are working with them. As has 
already been said, often they are working to  help other people wh ile they are dealing 
with personal issues in relation to their own circumstances. I also pay tribute to the 
Australian search and rescue parties w ho are already on the ground in Christchurch. 
Teams from the United States, Singapore, the United Kingdom, Japan, and Taiwan will 
be deployed as soon as  they get here. Offers of earthqu ake and rescue sp ecialists have 
also been received from Belgium, Israel , the European Union, Greece, Malaysia, 
Argentina, and France. The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian 
Affairs has offered assistance, and Internat ional Search and Rescue Advisory Group 
teams have been mobilised. An offer of assistance has been received from the United 
Nations Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific.  
As we consider this statement our t houghts are with the pe ople in Canterbury, 
particularly with those who have lost loved ones and with loved ones still missing.
